newsitem.title: CHINA: China motorcycle industry hurt by over-capacity.
newsitem.headline: China motorcycle industry hurt by over-capacity.

text.p: Overcapacity and rising stockpiles have badly hurt the profits of China's motorcycle producers and are causing a shakeout of the industry, company officials and the official press said on Friday.

The same story is being repeated across many sectors in China, including colour television, washing machines and refrigerators, where production has leapt ahead of demand, leading to price wars, idle plant and falling profits.
China's motorcycle output in 1996 will reach 9-10 million units, up from 7.83 million in 1995. But sales this year will be only about eight million, the Shanghai Securities News said on Friday.
Stockpiles reached 676,700 units in September, up from 233,400 at the end of 1995, it said.

China now has more than 200 motorcycle plants with total annual production capacity of 20 million units. Several new plants now under construction will add further capacity, each able to produce more than 500,000, the newspaper said.
A number of the motorcycle producers have A shares listed on the Shanghai or Shenzhen stock exchanges.

An official of one of them, Jinan Qinqi Motorcycles, said that by the end of this year or early next year, many small producers would be unable to survive, some would go bankrupt and others would be taken over.

"This transition will be as fast as it has been in the textile and consumer electronics sectors," he said. "Many companies started production, the market was saturated and then the small firms were taken over."

But an official of Changchun Gasoline Engine Corp said the rationalisation of the industry would take several years because many firms were supported by local governments that would not allow them to go bankrupt.
His company is based in Changchun, capital of the northeast province of Jilin.
The official said competition in the market was very fierce, but relatively less severe in his home northeast region because most producers were in south China.
China's motorcycle market has doubled in most years since 1990 but has now had entered a more normal growth stage, with rises in demand of 20-30 percent a year, he said.
Official figures show that China produced one million motorcycles in 1991, rising to three million in 1993, 5.22 million in 1994 and 7.83 million in 1995, making it the world's largest producer.
There are two motorcycles for every 10,000 people in China, against a world average of three and 17 in Japan, they show.

The Shanghai Securities News said the excess output had badly hit profit margins, with smaller producers already in the red. It said Beijing wants to slim the industry down to just 8-10 major producers.

"The current fierce competition and price cutting should in the long term benefit the motorcycle market, as it was doing in the colour television market, promoting strong firms and eliminating weak ones," the newspaper said.
